body:
Why additive manufacturing is useful

The main advantage of additive manufacturing is not simply that it uses a computer. It can make selected shapes, customised components and small batches without requiring a separate conventional mould for every design.

Its value is especially clear when a component has a complicated shape, when frequent design changes are necessary or when producing a small quantity by conventional methods would be expensive.

Design freedom and lightweight structures

Design freedom means the ability to manufacture shapes that may be difficult or costly to make using ordinary cutting or moulding. Additive manufacturing can create certain internal channels, hollow regions and lattice-like structures.

In a conventional assembly, several components might need separate manufacture and later joining. In some additive manufacturing applications, these features can be combined into a single printed part. This is sometimes called part consolidation.

Reducing unnecessary solid material may reduce component weight. However, a lighter design must still have the strength required for its intended function. An intricate shape is not automatically better or stronger.

Major application areas

Medical and dental applications

Human bodies differ in size and shape. Additive manufacturing can therefore be useful for patient-specific anatomical models, certain custom implants, prosthetic components and dental products.

For example, an anatomical model based on medical imaging may help a clinical team understand the shape of a patient's bone before a procedure. A properly designed and approved implant may be tailored to a particular patient, but its use requires appropriate medical evaluation and quality controls.

Bioprinting refers to research methods involving living cells or biological materials. It is being explored for tissue models and other medical applications. This must not be confused with routine hospital availability of fully functional, transplantable 3D-printed human organs.

Aerospace and space applications

Aircraft and spacecraft benefit from components that provide adequate strength while keeping weight low. Additive manufacturing can produce selected lightweight parts and complex internal features. It can also reduce the number of separate pieces needed in certain assemblies.

In May 2024, the Indian start-up Agnikul Cosmos launched Agnibaan-SOrTeD, which featured a single-piece additively manufactured semi-cryogenic rocket engine. This is an Indian example of the technology's use in space hardware, not evidence that every rocket engine is 3D-printed.

Industrial and manufacturing applications

  • Prototypes: Physical models for checking shape, appearance and fit before final production.
  • Jigs and fixtures: Special tools that help hold or position a component during manufacturing.
  • Replacement parts: Suitable components that may be produced when a particular design is needed in small quantities.
  • Complex components: Parts containing features that may require extensive machining or assembly if made conventionally.

Construction and the Gujarat connection

Large-scale 3D printing can deposit suitable construction materials according to a digital design. It may be used to form selected building elements, although construction still requires structural design, reinforcement where needed, foundations and compliance with applicable building requirements.

An official Government of India account published on 7 October 2026 described an Indian Army 2-storey 3D-printed dwelling unit in Ahmedabad, built over 12 weeks. This provides a direct Gujarat example of additive manufacturing beyond small plastic objects.

Limitations and practical trade-offs

Despite its advantages, 3D printing is not always the cheapest or fastest production method. The cost of machines and feedstock may be high, and individual objects may take considerable time to build. For very large production quantities of simple identical items, conventional moulding or other mass-production processes can remain more economical.

Printed objects can also have rough surfaces, internal defects or different strengths in different directions. Some parts need temporary support structures, finishing or extensive inspection. Powder handling, heated equipment and chemical resins also require suitable safety precautions.

A useful distinction: Additive manufacturing is often advantageous for complexity, customisation and small production runs. Conventional manufacturing may have an advantage for high-volume production of simple, standardised products.

Prelims focus

  • Rapid prototyping and patient-specific products are important additive manufacturing applications.
  • Part consolidation means combining features or pieces into fewer manufactured parts.
  • Aerospace applications may benefit from reduced component weight.
  • Agnibaan-SOrTeD was launched in May 2024 with a single-piece additively manufactured engine.
  • An Indian Army 2-storey 3D-printed dwelling unit was reported at Ahmedabad.
  • Trap: Printing biological tissue models does not mean that fully functional transplantable organs are routinely available.

[Sources: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Additive Manufacturing Part Qualification, sections Summary and What is the Problem?, updated 26 March 2025, consulted 14 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Additive Manufacturing in India, sections Space and Aerospace, Defence, Healthcare and Construction, 7 October 2026, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Separate manufactured pieces are contrasted with 1 integrated part containing internal features, with functional strength still required.
pictures.caption: Additive manufacturing can produce complex structures while reducing the need for separate parts.

title: Applications, Design Freedom and Limitations of 3D Printing

body:
Why quality cannot be judged only by appearance

A printed object may look correct but still fail during use. The outside shape does not always reveal weak bonding between layers, internal pores or defects caused by inconsistent processing.

This is especially important in medical, aerospace and other safety-related applications. A component used in a critical application must satisfy the relevant performance and safety requirements, regardless of how it is manufactured.

Quality assurance and quality control

Quality assurance (QA) means organising and controlling the manufacturing process so that required quality can be achieved consistently. Quality control (QC) means checking whether a material, process output or finished component meets specified requirements.

For example, recording the approved printing procedure and establishing procedures for checking the suitability of incoming material are quality-assurance activities. Measuring the finished component and examining it for defects are quality-control activities. The two work together rather than being interchangeable.

Where quality problems may arise

StagePossible concernPurpose of control
FeedstockContaminated or unsuitable powder, filament or resin.Ensure material identity and consistent properties.
Printing processIncorrect temperature, energy input or material deposition.Keep the process within approved conditions.
Printed componentIncorrect dimensions, poor surface finish or internal pores.Check that the component meets requirements.
Finishing and documentationIncomplete curing, finishing or production records.Confirm readiness for use and trace the manufacturing history.

Important properties and checks

  • Dimensional accuracy: Whether the manufactured component has the required measurements and shape.
  • Mechanical properties: Whether strength and related characteristics are suitable for the intended load.
  • Surface finish: Whether the surface meets the required condition.
  • Internal soundness: Whether harmful pores or other hidden defects are present.
  • Repeatability: Whether repeated production can deliver consistent results.
  • Traceability: Whether the material, machine, process and production records can be identified when required.

Anisotropy means that a material's properties differ according to direction. Some additively manufactured parts can have different strengths along and across their layers. The amount and importance of this difference depend on the material and manufacturing process.

Standards relevant to 3D printing

International standards help establish common terminology and organised quality requirements.

  • ISO/ASTM 52900:2021: Establishes fundamental terminology and concepts for additive manufacturing. The 2021 edition was reviewed and confirmed in 2025.
  • ISO/ASTM 52920:2023: Specifies qualification-related requirements for industrial additive manufacturing processes and production sites. Its scope concerns process and production quality assurance, independent of the specific material and manufacturing method.

Quality-management standards such as ISO 9001 apply to organisational quality-management systems. ISO 13485 concerns quality-management systems for medical devices. These are not alternative names for the 3D-printing process categories. ISO/ASTM 52920:2023 provides additive-manufacturing-specific requirements in addition to applicable quality-management requirements.

Following a manufacturing standard does not automatically certify every finished product. A medical implant, aircraft component or other critical item may require further testing, regulatory approval or formal qualification for its intended use.

Prelims focus

  • QA controls the process; QC checks whether requirements have been met.
  • Anisotropy means that properties can differ with direction.
  • ISO/ASTM 52900:2021 concerns additive manufacturing fundamentals and vocabulary.
  • ISO/ASTM 52920:2023 concerns industrial additive manufacturing process and production-site qualification requirements.
  • ISO 9001 is a general quality-management standard; ISO 13485 concerns medical-device quality management.
  • Trap: A visually correct printed object is not necessarily qualified for safety-critical use.

[Sources: ISO, ISO/ASTM 52900:2021, abstract and publication status, consulted 14 November 2026; ISO, ISO/ASTM 52920:2023, abstract and scope, published June 2023, consulted 14 November 2026; National Institute of Standards and Technology, Additive Manufacturing Part Qualification, sections Summary, What is the Problem? and Objective, updated 26 March 2025, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: QA spans feedstock, manufacturing, the finished component and records, with QC conformance checks throughout.
pictures.caption: Quality assurance covers the material, manufacturing process, finished part and production record.

title: Quality Assurance, Testing and Standards in Additive Manufacturing

body:
What is advanced manufacturing?

Advanced manufacturing uses modern machines, digital systems, automation and improved production methods to manufacture goods with greater control, consistency or flexibility. Its purpose is not limited to replacing manual work; it also includes improving product quality, safety, efficiency and the ability to manufacture different products.

A factory can use both conventional and advanced manufacturing methods. For example, metal may still be cut from a solid block, but the cutting machine may be digitally programmed, fitted with sensors and connected to other equipment.

Computer numerical control

Computer numerical control (CNC) is the control of a machine's movements and operations through programmed numerical instructions.

In a CNC machining centre, a computer program controls the movement of tools and the workpiece. Operations can include cutting, drilling and milling. The main benefit is the ability to repeat specified movements with consistent control.

A CNC machine is not necessarily an industrial robot. It is a machine controlled by a programmed system. Many CNC machines are used for subtractive manufacturing, although computer-controlled equipment may also be used in additive and other processes.

Industrial robotics

An industrial robot is a programmable, automatically controlled machine capable of carrying out industrial tasks through mechanical movements. A common example is a robotic arm that moves a component from one station to another or performs welding.

Industrial robots can be used for:

  • Welding and painting.
  • Picking, placing and packaging components.
  • Material handling between machines.
  • Assembly and selected inspection tasks.

A robot does not necessarily make decisions independently. Many industrial robots repeatedly follow defined programmes. More capable systems may use sensor feedback to adapt certain actions.

Sensors, controllers and actuators

Automation becomes more responsive when machines can detect changes in their surroundings or operating conditions.

  • Sensor: Detects or measures a physical quantity, such as temperature, pressure, vibration, position or the presence of an object.
  • Controller: Uses programmed instructions and, where available, sensor information to decide what action is required.
  • Actuator: Carries out an action, such as moving a motor, opening a valve or operating a mechanical mechanism.

For example, a sensor on a production line may detect that a component has reached the correct position. The controller then sends a signal to a robotic arm to pick it up.

Open-loop and feedback control

In an open-loop system, the controller performs an action without using a measurement of the resulting output to correct it. A simple timed operation can work in this manner.

In a closed-loop or feedback-control system, the actual result is measured and compared with the required result. The controller can then make a correction. For example, a temperature-controlled industrial oven can use a sensor to measure temperature and adjust heating.

Feedback can improve accuracy and consistency, but it depends on suitable sensors, correct settings and functioning equipment.

How the technologies work together

An automated production line may combine a CNC machine, robotic material handling, inspection sensors and a central control system. One machine shapes a component, a robot transfers it and a sensor checks its position or dimensions.

The purpose of integration is to reduce unnecessary delays, improve consistency and allow workers to supervise a larger or more complex manufacturing process. Human supervision remains necessary for safety, maintenance and decisions beyond the automated system's capabilities.

Prelims focus

  • CNC means computer numerical control.
  • Many CNC machining operations are subtractive.
  • Industrial robots are programmable machines used for industrial tasks.
  • A sensor detects or measures; an actuator performs an action.
  • Feedback control uses measured output to help correct the system.
  • Trap: A robot and a CNC machine are not identical technologies, although they may operate together.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Industries, printed pp. 50–52, sections Industries and Industrial System; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Manufacturing Industries, printed pp. 85–86, discussion of manufacturing and industrial inputs; National Institute of Standards and Technology, Kibira and Shao, Data Requirements for a Digital Twin of a CNC Machine Tool, abstract, published 29 January 2026, consulted 14 November 2026.]
